summary: Details considerations on how IoT devices use IP addresses and DNS names, which matter more as operators deploy Manufacturer Usage Descriptions (RFC 8520) to control device access. It also recommends when and how to use DNS names in MUD files.

eli5.summary: Smart gadgets look up names to reach servers. Rules limiting where gadgets can go are easier if the gadgets name things in sensible ways, and this gives advice.

subtitle: How IoT makers should use DNS names so that network firewalls driven by MUD files can actually enforce them.

tldr.problem: A MUD file can allow a device to reach servers by DNS name, but the firewall that enforces it only sees IP addresses, so names must be turned into addresses ahead of time and the answers often differ.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models how a MUD controller resolves names, lists DNS habits that break it (address literals, unpredictable CDN names, overly generic names), and gives five recommendations to manufacturers.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice: use DNS names consistently, keep them under the manufacturer's control, prefer stable CDN names, avoid tailored answers and use the DNS servers the network hands out.

today: RFC 9726 is a Best Current Practice published in March 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the MUD specification in RFC 8520.

sections.title: Names in MUD Files, Addresses on the Wire
sections.content:
RFC 8520 lets a manufacturer publish a Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) file. Its Access Control Lists (ACLs) can permit a device to reach Internet resources by DNS name or by IP address.

Names have advantages: they can change over time, cover IPv4 and IPv6, and support load balancing, including multi-CDN setups. The catch is the enforcement point, typically a firewall, which sees only Layer 3 headers: source and destination IP addresses and, unless IPsec encrypts them, the UDP or TCP port. The DNS name is not present. So some component has to map the names in the ACL to IP addresses.
sections.eli5: The rule list says website names, but the guard at the gate can only read house numbers. Someone has to look up which numbers go with which names.

sections.title: How a MUD Controller Maps Names to Addresses
sections.content:
The simplest working strategy for a MUD controller is a forward lookup of each name, then using the resulting addresses to fill in the ACLs. The model is non-normative; it exists so manufacturers understand how their names will be resolved.

The hard part is that the mapping can be non-deterministic. Round-robin DNS (RFC 1794) returns A or AAAA records in a different order each time. That is harmless while every address is returned, but it fails when geographic load balancing returns only some addresses, when a reply is too big and gets truncated, or when the list changes between the controller's lookup and the device's lookup.

To compensate, the controller repeats lookups regularly, rate-limited to spare the DNS servers. It does best when it asks the same caching recursive resolver as the device: geographic decisions then match, the answer stays stable for the advertised TTL, and any omitted round-robin addresses are omitted for both. That is easy in a residential CPE device, where the controller, enforcement point and resolver share one box and one reboot. It is harder in an enterprise or cloud SDN, where the controller may not know the device's resolver or be allowed to query it.

A critical failure occurs when the device gets a new address set but the controller's copy has not yet reached its TTL: the ACLs hold old addresses and the connection fails.
sections.eli5: The guard writes down the house numbers for each name. If the name's houses change and the guard's list is old, the gadget gets stopped at the gate.

sections.title: Anti-Patterns for IoT Manufacturers
sections.content:
The RFC lists things manufacturers have been observed doing that give MUD enforcement trouble.

IP address literals

A firmware update service may return a URL with a bare IP address, hoping to avoid DNS problems. But the server must then pick IPv4 or IPv6, and a device behind NAT64 can usually reach an IPv4 server by name (through DNS64) but not an arbitrary IPv4 address. A MUD file would need constant updates as addresses change. TLS certificates are harder to get for an IP address, and a literal in the TLS Server Name Indication cannot tell a server which tenant is wanted.

Non-deterministic names

A control protocol may point to content at third-party CDN or cloud-storage names that the manufacturer does not choose and that change faster than a MUD file can be updated. The suggested fix is a stable name in the manufacturer's own zone with a CNAME to the CDN, which the controller can follow and refresh by TTL. If the full set of servers is known, the manufacturer may instead list the addresses directly.

Names that are too generic

A single name serving all customers' content looks ideal for MUD, but a compromised device could then reach any customer's bucket. MUD ACLs permit hostnames and ports only; they cannot filter URLs.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets use raw house numbers, or names that a delivery company invents on the fly, or one giant name for the whole town. Each of these makes the guard's job impossible or risky.

sections.title: Recommendations for Manufacturers
sections.content:
Section 6 is the core. Adding a MUD file is operationally simple: a small DHCP client change, or a QR code on the packaging (RFC 9238). The difficult part is deciding what goes in the file, which means reviewing the device's network communications.

  • Consistently use DNS. Avoid IP address literals in any protocol.
  • Use primary names controlled by the manufacturer. Make them aliases pointing at production systems, ideally one name per logical function so rules can be switched on and off. Many aliases and wildcard certificates are no longer costly.
  • Use a CDN with stable names. Very low TTLs make it harder for the controller to see the device's answer. A CDN that always returns the same A and AAAA set, just permuted, is more reliable.
  • Do not use tailored responses. Answers that vary by client location (for example using the edns-client-subnet option of RFC 7871) are hard to reproduce when the device uses a different connection, firewall or resolver. This is a strong recommendation.
  • Prefer DNS servers learned from DHCP or Router Advertisements. Public resolvers are discouraged, whether Do53, DoQ, DoT or DoH.
sections.eli5: The advice is simple: always use names, use names you own, pick delivery companies with steady names, do not hand out different answers to different people, and ask the local network for directions.

sections.title: Resolver Choice, Privacy and Local Discovery
sections.content:
Using DoT, DoH or DoQ, or an outside public resolver, can hide queries from the local network but breaks the controller's assumption that it sees the same answers. If a device does not use the DHCP or Router Advertisement servers, the controller must be told which it uses, and there is no protocol for that yet. Until one exists, the best practice is to always use the servers provided by the network.

If a device might ever fall back to a non-local resolver, that should happen only when the local ones give no answer to any query, repeatedly. Those resolver addresses and their ports (53, 853 for DoT, 443 for DoH) must then be permitted in the MUD file.

The privacy section notes that non-local servers expose the list of names to third parties, that encrypted DNS still exposes it to the server operator, and that unencrypted local DNS exposes it to internal eavesdroppers. Regular update checks reveal that a particular manufacturer's device is present, so manufacturers are encouraged to anonymize update queries, for example with a third-party notification service or DNSSEC-signed TXT records carried over DoT or DoH.

Multicast DNS and DNS-SD can also lead a device to external hosts, or to internal connections a MUD controller never heard of. Internal communications are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If a gadget asks a stranger for directions, the stranger learns where it is going, and the guard cannot check the answer. Best to ask the local helper, and keep update questions private.

sections.title: Security and the Cost of Bad MUD Files
sections.content:
The RFC sees two requirements in tension: operators want to manage devices with MUD, and devices need network resources that may be critical to their safe operation. It argues they need not conflict, but careful planning of DNS use is required.

An inaccurate MUD file causes spurious security exceptions. Repeated false alarms can lead to the whole exception process being turned off, so that even legitimate alerts are ignored. Accurate MUD files may need significant rework of key systems so that all required network access can be described. Manufacturers are told that files that are good enough beat perfect ones, and that if in doubt they should be somewhat more permissive if that yields no spurious alerts.

An appendix explains why the alternative of mapping IP addresses back to names in real time fails: reverse lookups are too slow, reveal usage patterns, are often incomplete, and cannot cope with wildcard names.
sections.eli5: If the gadget's rule list is wrong, the alarm keeps ringing for no reason, and soon people switch the alarm off. So the list has to be accurate.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 9726 was published in March 2025 as BCP 241, a Best Current Practice. It has no IANA actions. The recommendations apply to devices described by MUD files as defined in RFC 8520.
sections.eli5: This is an official how-to guide that the community agreed on in 2025.

items.title: Consistently use DNS
items.text: No IP address literals in any protocol.

items.title: Own your names
items.text: Aliases in the manufacturer's zone, one per function.

items.title: Stable CDN names
items.text: Avoid very low TTLs; permuted but constant record sets are best.

items.title: No tailored answers
items.text: Location-dependent replies are hard for a controller to match.

items.title: Local DNS servers
items.text: Use servers learned from DHCP or Router Advertisements.
